utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those watching and listening our proceedings. We apologise for the late commencement of the trial today. There were some unforeseeable circumstances which -- which caused this problem. Are there any procedural matters to raise at the beginning of today's hearing? I don't see anybody on his feet. Then the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rutten, Mr. McCloskey for the Prosecution is commencing his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you first tell us your name and your rank.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My name is Jan Rutten and my rank is lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have testified both in the Popovic case and in the Krstic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked those same questions that you were asked in those cases, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, my answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you testify in those cases truthfully?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. President, I would like to offer the testimony of the colonel in the Popovic -- the Popovic case, which is 65 ter 7137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7137 shall be assigned Exhibit P2629. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would also like to add -- offer all the documents under the next heading associated exhibits starting at 65 ter 7138, ending with 3361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that two of them are already in evidence. This is P1506 and P1491. All the others will be received as exhibits and given a P number by internal memorandum by the Registry to save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. President, I now have a -- a summary to read, and -- given the importance of this witness, the four-hour estimate of the Defence, and the summary is a bit longer than normal, but I do not have any intention of asking the colonel any questions, so this should be the Prosecution's main presentation, this summary, aside from allowing the colonel to give us a brief update now before I get to the summary of his career since he's last testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, can you just give us a brief update on your career since the time you testified a while back in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Since the end of 2006, I was stationed in Munster, Germany, in the 1st German Netherlands Corps as head of personnel affairs over there. And during that period up to now, I was in a mission abroad in Iraq, Baghdad, for the NTMI mission, NATO training mission Iraq, during the elections in Iraq in 2010. After that and during -- and the period before, I also was stationed in Germany and had a job as a brigade personnel affairs officer for the 1st German Netherlands Corps over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and we're glad you made it back from Iraq looking healthy.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to read to a summary and if I get anything wrong, you can - I'm sure as you will - correct me if I have made a mistake. Colonel Rutten testified in the Krstic trial as a viva voce witness and as a result 92 ter witness in the Popovic trial. This summary reflects both trials. The colonel joined the Royal Dutch Army in 1979 as a conscript and served as non-commissioned officer in a variety of posts and places until 1991, when he entered the officers' training school which he completed in 1993 where he was commissioned as a 2nd lieutenant, and he served with the 41st Armoured Infantry Battalion. In 1994, he began his service with the 11th Air Mobile Brigade as an anti-tank platoon commander, and subsequently as a deputy commanding officer of a company. From January through July 1995, he served with DutchBat III as a 1st lieutenant during which time he was a patrol co-ordinator and intelligence officer for Charlie Company. During the seven months then Lieutenant Rutten served with DutchBat III. He saw and learned of a decreasing movement of convoys to the enclave by the Serb forces. The decrease in the number of UNHCR convoys began around the end of February or beginning of March, and the supplies in the warehouse in Srebrenica were getting lower. There was not enough food for the civilian population, and the situation in the enclave became so bad that people would go through DutchBat's garbage when it was taken to the dump site. He identified a photograph he took while on patrol of civilians surrounding the dump truck. The DutchBat also had to minimise its consumption of supplies, and this became more severe at the beginning of March. In addition, from April onwards, DutchBat did not have enough personnel for its activities within the enclave since the Serbs did not allow Dutch soldiers who had been on leave to return. DutchBat was also insufficiently armed as it had not received sufficient ammunition supplies and that the ammunition was not safe any more and needed to be replenished. On 10 July 1995, he heard severe impacts behind the compound from a rocket launcher based in Bratunac. Following the shelling, they found an unexploded rocket just behind the compound; that is, DutchBat did. The shelling became heavier in the following days and stopped during the late evening. Colonel Rutten's view of the purpose of the shelling was to intimidate DutchBat from leaving the compound and as an act of terror. On Monday evening after the attack began, he and others heard from Bravo Company that the situation in Srebrenica was getting out of hand and that refugees were on the move towards Potocari. He then received an order to cut a hole in the rear side of the compound fence to let the refugees in, if necessary. Bravo Company soldiers arrived on the evening of 10th July with the first refugees who were kept at the bus compound, or as the colonel called it, the bus remise, because he had not received an order permitting them on the compound and he closed up the fence again. On Tuesday, the 11th of July, Lieutenant Rutten was ordered to re-open the hole in the fence. Lieutenant Koster led a group of DutchBat soldiers at the bus remise. At this time, he, Lieutenant Rutten heard that a large group of refugees were heading towards Potocari and that Bravo Company had to leave Srebrenica because of the shelling and the chaos there. The first group of refugees began arriving at the rear side guided by Koster and his men at the bus remise. Refugees arrived all day on the 11th until approximately 5.00 or 6.00 in the evening at which time Lieutenant Rutten was ordered not to let in my more refugees because the factory hall itself was completely filled. He was then ordered by Major Otter to form three groups of ten men to secure the area of the bus remise where the refugees were. There were many refugees in that area, and they placed white tape around the whole area as the only means available to make it clear that it was meant to be a secure area under UN surveillance. On the morning of 12 July 1995, small-arms fire was followed by mortar fire and Serb soldiers set fire to houses in the area near the location of the refugees. The first Serb soldiers to arrive were described by the witness as more or less Rambo types. He informed one of the Serb soldiers who looked like the leader that they could not cross the tape because it was UN territory. That Serb soldier just laughed and stepped over the tape, as did others. Serb soldiers then stole equipment and personal items belonging to his men securing the bus compound. On 12 July, Lieutenant Rutten saw General Mladic and his body-guards arrive followed by a truck carrying bread and a fire truck with water. The distribution of bread, water and candy was filmed. Immediately after the filming stopped, the handing out of the bread, water and candy stopped. The Serb forces even took back some of it from the refugees. He did not see the Serb forces distribute anything else after that to the refugees on 12 or 13 July. Later on 12 July as the buses were arriving, Serb soldiers threatened him to give up his weapon, flak vest and radio sets. He refused and told the soldiers that he needed to speak to their commander. Subsequently, a Serb soldier who appeared to be a commander arrived and again demanded the equipment while another Serb soldier grabbed Lieutenant Rutten's weapon. He again refused until the soldier pointed a gun at his head and demanded his radio set. He then gave up one of his radio sets and used the other to inform his superior office that he'd lost his weapon to the VRS. His men then also gave up their weapons and vests at gunpoint. He and his men were then taken to the bus compound and placed under guard by two Serb soldiers. He protested to a man he identified in a photograph as Captain Mane that he -- that he was being held and that they had lost their equipment, but Captain Mane sent him back to the rest of the group. When Captain Mane returned a few hours later, Captain Mane sent Lieutenant Rutten and his squad of ten men escorted by two Serb soldiers back to the compound where they spent the night. On the morning of 13 July, he was on duty in the Operations Room where he heard that Lieutenant Versteeg saw two buses loaded with men leave the vicinity of the white house. He ordered Versteeg to follow the two buses because they were not leaving with the larger group of buses along the road. Versteeg followed the bus to Bratunac, then radioed that it was not going to Kladanj but turned in another direction and that he was being instructed by Serb soldiers from following the bus. Lieutenant Rutten instructed Versteeg to follow the bus, but the Serbs grabbed Versteeg's car and then hijacked it. Consequently, he never learned where those buses went. Because of this incident with Versteeg, Lieutenant Rutten decided to go to the white house himself under the pretext of delivering a wheelbarrow with packages of water, and he was accompanied by a sergeant major. At the gate at the entrance to the white house he saw a huge pile of rucksacks and belongings. A few metres further were all kinds of identity cards and passports on the ground. The white house was well guarded by Serb soldiers who refused them entry, but he went around the side of the house and managed to get in. Once inside he saw a Muslim man hanging from the staircase by one arm, so he asked the Serb soldier to lower him to the ground. While this was being done, he tried to enter a room on the right side from which he'd heard voices but was prevented by a Serb soldier in a green uniform who -- using a gun to prevent him from going in. He then stepped outside and saw a Serb soldier at the gate telling men arriving at the house to throw down their things, and a few metres later telling them to throw their identity cards. Lieutenant Rutten went back inside and upstairs where he found two rooms filled with 50 men and boys from age 12 to 55. He photographed both groups of people but stopped because a Serb soldier was arriving with more. He then left the house. It was clear to him that this was no normal interrogation as normal procedure with POWs would require a system of identifying the prisoners; whereas, it was very clear to him that the men in the white house would not need their IDs or belongings. Later that evening, the Serbs set fire to the belongings and IDs which were outside the house. The fire burned for two days. He identified a photograph he took of the smoke rising from the fire. He did not see any signs of violence or torture during the times he visited the white house. After leaving the white house he went to an area where Lieutenant van Duijn was posted with a blockade of four APCs. At that location, a local interpreter informed him that there were rumours that men had been killed near a well on the road on the Budak side. He, Sergeant Major van Schaik, and Koster then passed through the APC blockade and followed a dirt road. In a very bushy area they found a small stream on the left behind a house near a meadow. As soon as they saw the meadow they saw some bodies lying nearby the stream. He inspected the bodies which were nine men in civilian clothes lying with their faces towards the stream. All had small calibre gunshots to their backs. The men were approximately 45 to 55 years old. He touched the bodies which were warm. The blood was still running and there were no flies on them yet. In his view they had not been shot long before that time, and he said that there were no evidence that the bodies had been moved to that location. He told van Schaik to pick up the identification that was on the grass in front of the bodies and he took a photograph of Koster kneeling between the bodies. He also photographed all nine bodies. At that point there was firing in their direction. He told van Schaik to drop all the identification which he had picked up and they had to leave. He reported that what he had seen -- he reported what he had seen to Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans who told him he would pass his report up to a higher level. When he returned to Holland he turned his camera over to someone from the army intelligence branch but was later informed that something had happened during the development and the photos were never developed or seen. Back in Potocari he then remained at the blockade where he took some pictures of what the Serbs were doing and observed a DutchBat lieutenant and some DutchBat soldiers actually what he viewed as assisting in the deportation of the population by doing their best to help the Muslim refugees leave the area. Because there were Serb soldiers sitting all along the road with their weapons, Lieutenant-Colonel Rutten felt that Dutch was helping in this process. He told this to Lieutenant van Duijn who had a different point of view and was just trying to help the refugees move out of the area. On the other side of the line at the buses, Serb soldiers were carrying out the separation of men from their families. UN soldiers were not working with the refugees at the point where the men were being separated from the women. The witness clearly saw the separation of men from the women and children. He was then ordered by his company commander to escort the last bus that was leaving. He and his driver prepared a jeep and parked it next to the compound entrance while waiting for the last buses to leave. As they waited, he told his driver to accompany them back to the white house so that he could have as many witnesses as possible. By that time, the pile of belongings was huge and many more IDs and passports were laying on the ground. They went to the previously empty left side of the house and saw two Serb soldiers on the staircase which was filled with Muslim men. He could see the total fear on the faces of the Muslim men and boys. They then walked back to the front of the house and saw the balcony totally filled with men and boys. He estimates that almost 300 men were in the house and on its balcony. By the time it was clear that the last buses were filled up later in the day on the 13th, the battalion had stopped escorting convoys because it was no use any more in his view. He asked his company ops room if he could make an attempt to escort the last buses and was given the okay. So he quickly drove to the head of the convoy which was heading towards OP Papa. After driving approximately 1 to 1.5 kilometres, a private car containing three Serb soldiers in green camouflage uniforms came up behind him. Next another car containing two Serb soldiers came up from the side of the road and blocked the road. The Serb soldiers pointed their weapons at them. The actions of the two cars appeared well organised. At his instruction, his driver then made a U-turn and returned to the compound. As a result, the convoy was not escorted. When he returned to the compound he was told to accompany a truck and some medical personnel who were going into Srebrenica to pick up the last elderly people left behind along the road. En route he was stopped by Serb soldiers who ordered him, his driver and a sergeant in the back seat out at gunpoint. The Serb soldiers told him that they would have to continue on in the truck. When they reached the Bravo Company compound, he saw Serbs looting the compound and driving Dutch APCs filled with stolen material. The Serbs had also emptied the weapons collection point. Along the road they found a few elderly people whom they placed in the back of the truck and took back to Potocari with them. There were several more days in Potocari, as you know, but I will stop the summary there and turn the witness over to General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it that there are no questions during the examination-in-chief by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And I -- as you recognise, there was a bit more detail, and I think that has helped save us some time and hopefully be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, Judge Nyambe wants to put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just a few clarifications. Before the Defence starts asking you questions, I just need some clarifications. The first one is at page 11, lines 5 to 8, the statement reads: "The battalion had stopped escorting convoys because it was no use any more in his view." "In his view" means "in your view." "And he asked his company ops room if he could make an attempt to escort the last buses and was given the okay. So he quickly drove to the head of the convoy which was heading towards OP Papa." I have some difficult to appreciate just how the sequence of events took place with regard to the escort of the convoy. You have said you were of the view that battalion had stopped escorting convoy because in your view because it was of no use any more, and yet in the next minute you are seen ordered -- actually, you are seen asking if you could make an attempt to escort the last buses after you've already made that -- that conclusion that it is of no use. So can you please just explain the sequence of events, how it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's no problem. It looks like now the sequence is that it looks minutes later, but it took quite some time to fill up the buses and trucks with people. Approximately 60 till 70 persons were on a bus or a truck, and there was a long line of trucks and waiting before it was filled up, so it was quite some time in between. The moment I saw an opportunity to -- to get -- to escort the total convoy as it was leaving, so there was some more time in between than it looks like here now in the summary. And it was to my own judgement that I heard from my company commander. So if there is a possibility, please take the opportunity and try to -- to escort these convoy. It was one of the last convoys that was leaving with the last people, so that could be an opportunity then to follow them as much as possible to get a clear view of was -- of what was happening with the refugees that left the -- the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: The clarification I'm looking from you is the impression created as if the idea to escort the convoy was your own. You gave up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was my own. We had to -- to make an estimation whether it was meaningful or even possible to try to escort the convoys because we -- we lost a lot of vehicles and personnel to try to escort previous convoys that left the enclave. So -- and our people were held on the road two Kladanj in several houses, and I -- I was known before that a lot of DutchBat members were held there. So -- but we need to had a clear view of what was really happening with the people, so that was the reason that I made another attempt to -- to escort the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Forgive me. Then at line -- page 10, line 13 to 16, you are said to have said UN soldiers were not working with the refugees at the point where the women were being separated from the men. Why were UN soldiers not working with the refugees? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean with this -- with this question, because there were -- with the APC blocking where Lieutenant van Duijn was there were UN soldiers there, but it was not my specific job to work with my men and the men under my command to assist Lieutenant van Duijn at the APC blocking. We were free. We had free movement, so we tried to make an estimate of what was happening exactly near the white house and tried to get an overview to -- to inform my company commander of what was really happening outside the gate. So the question that you're answering is to me not that clear, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to rephrase my question. In the context of what you've just said, you have said UN soldiers were not working with the refugees at the point where the men were being separated from the women. By your statement, I understand that the UN soldiers were supposed to be working with the refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't think that we were working -- my men were not working with the refugees, because it was not our job to collect the refugees and brought them to the buses -- and bring them to the buses. That was my point of view, and that was in fact the basis of the argument that I had with my colleagues Lieutenant van Duijn. So if you're aiming at that, that's a different situation. Working together with the refugees does not mean that we were not helping them or assisting them. We were there to -- just to monitor what was happening, in my view, and not to be active in the role to help them get -- to get out of the enclave. That was not our job. That was not our mandate, and that's perhaps the difference in view on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Somewhere you have said you opened the hole in -- in some building --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. It was -- sorry if I'm interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the rear side of the compound. There was a small river and there was a bridge over that river, and that was connected with a small dirt road to the bus remise. There were a lot of refugees collecting also the evening earlier. So we tried the evening earlier to make a hole in the fence that if it was necessary, that we could immediately start to transfer the refugees to the compound itself, but in the evening it was not necessary already, so we closed the fence later on the evening. The next day, we opened the fence because the pressure was getting too much and we let in approximately 4- to 5.000 refugees on the compound and they stayed in the factory itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your action to assist the refugees to come in and enclose and open the following day, does that -- was that part of your mandate as you say you were monitoring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was part of our mandate, because our mandate was to protect the civilians of the enclave of Srebrenica, and at that point it was quite clear that there was a lot of pressure coming on the bus remise and Serbian soldiers were coming in. So there was a larger threat to the refugees themselves. So that was the moment I checked by my superiors the next day and I said, "We have to leave in now the refugees," because I got the message from the other colleagues that were on the bus remise, and they said there were more refugees and the pressure was getting higher and higher. And that was the point that we left and that we leave -- we opened the hole again and we left in the -- the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just one last question. At page, I think, 10, lines 9 to 11, you are saying: Lieutenant-Colonel Rutten felt that Dutch was helping in this process. He told this to Lieutenant van Duijn who had a different point of view and was just trying to help the refugees move out of the area. Can you clarify the difference of opinion between you and the other lieutenant on this issue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that process I was also making photographs of what was happening near the line of buses and trucks and on those photos clearly were some Serb -- Serbs that I photographed, this I make a picture of, and looking through the camera it was not a nice view that UN soldiers were, in fact, it looked like if they were in fact helping the evacuation of the refugees from the enclave, and that was surely at that point not in our mandate, because if you can't escort the convoys any more, it's out of hand. You're not in control any more, and that was the reason that I saw that there was a larger trap to the refugees when they left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has another question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The interpretation continued so far. That's why I'm waiting with the question. Witness, Colonel Rutten, I with like to ask you something about the photos. When you returned to the Netherlands, you handed over your camera to an army officer who told you that later they were unable to develop the photographs. I would like to ask you if you have kept any photographs of the events you recorded after you left the white house when you encountered Lieutenant van Duijn and by the roadside Budak. Do you mean to say that you have no photos left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a second roll of -- film roll of photos that I took along also to the Netherlands, and I handed in only one film roll with the specific photos I earlier spoke about of the nine killed persons, but the other photos I handed also a few of them in here to the court itself in earlier cases; for instance, the photograph of the garbage truck on it, and some other photos of burning of the documents outside of the white house. I have some other photos, but they are actually of no interest. That was -- that were the photos on the second film roll. The photos on the first film roll, they were the ones that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The photo of the garbage truck and the burning materials were within the -- the exhibits mentioned that he had identified in the previous trial, and they -- I can -- I think they're marked in -- in the exhibits, but I can double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one -- just one more question, I promise. I just need to come back to the issue of the photographs. At page 9 of today's transcript, you are stated as having said: "He also photographed all nine bodies and at that point there was firing in their direction. He told van --" I'm sorry, I can't pronounce the surname, "to drop all the identification which he had to pick up and they had to leave." I want you to clarify a bit about the issue of you telling the other gentleman who was with you to drop all the identification which were picked from the nine bodies. Can you clarify what was going on in your mind when you asked him to drop all the identifications and leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not in the summary before that Mr. McCloskey gave, but the thing is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, it was in the summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it was in the summary, but not the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry for that. But not the explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. That is the reason for the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason was that we -- we got fired at us, and at the same moment I was taking the last picture, and you can tell whether the firing is quite close or not, and it was quite close. I then gave immediately the order to drop the -- the documents, because we had to go through the line with the APCs where the Serbs were to get back to the compound, and so it felt not safe of having documents with us when we had to go through that line again back to the compound. And we actually got to -- got through that line by picking up one of the stretchers where one of the wounded people was on, and it looked like to the other ones that we were helping to bring a stretcher along, when in fact we were at the other side of the line and we saw something that might had some effect later on and that was the -- the things that we saw with the -- with the nine bodies. So it was to me it felt unsecure to have documents on us of Muslim people that were killed already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn to commence your cross-examination, to put questions to the witness. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish peace unto this house. I wish that this day in court and the whole proceedings end in keeping with God's will, not mine. I would like to welcome Colonel Rutten and wish him a pleasant stay with us in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, let's begin with the last question when you were asked why you discarded the documents of the nine people killed. My question is: Why did you throw away evidence that nine people had been killed? Was there any other reason other than fear from the people at the check-point considering that you should have let the Serb side know as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was not -- you mean -- you used the word "fear." It was not fear. I used another word, and I -- and it was secure and unsecure, and we felt unsecure to get through the Serb line to get to our own people again. It was pure a matter of protecting my two colleagues and myself to get back again, and I'm well aware that it was evidence, but this is a decision that you have to make in a split second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, could you tell the Trial Chamber was your task to protect yourselves or to protect the refugees and the evidence? Why did you throw it away? What would have Serbs done to you if they had seen passports on you? They could have only seized them. Did you fear something else? Did you feel something else would happen, or was there any other reason why you discarded the passports? Were there some real reasons or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir's microphone be adjusted so he speaks closer into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I count about five questions in that group and that's, I think, just too much for anyone to have to go through. If he could break it down, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed, Mr. Tolimir. Quite a lot of questions in one, and therefore it's much better to split it up and to put one question after the other, and please avoid repetitions. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Was your task to protect refugees and to record all incidents, and did you have to throw away passports which were evidence of the incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Our task was to protect refugees but not at all costs, and I considered that as an unsecure situation. So that was the reason that I gave the order to the sergeant major to throw away these documents. But then again, were they of any significance later on, because in front of the white house your people were collecting the documents and working permits and passports from the Muslim people themselves, so -- and they were burned afterwards. So, yeah, I don't see the -- the reason of that question then, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. On page 8 of today's transcript, line 10, if I could note it down well because you spoke faster than the court reporter, you said: "And he saw that people were throwing onto the ground everything they were carrying." Did prisoners of war also throw away everything on the ground themselves, and did they also discard their IDs, passports, like you did?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Sir, it's not quite clear to me what people you are referring to. Do you mean the Muslim people, or do you mean other people, because that's not quite clear in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could the colonel be shown the transcript on page 8 beginning with line 10. If I noted it down well, because I don't know the language and the court reporter does not always follow the speakers, and it says -- Mr. McCloskey was speaking: "And he saw people throwing onto the ground everything they were carrying. He photographed both groups going behind the house." That was page 8, Mr. McCloskey speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to assist you. On page 8, line 12 through 14. I read, I quote: "He then stepped outside and saw a Serb soldier at the gate telling men arriving at the house to throw down their things, and a few metres later telling them to throw their identity cards." This is slightly different from what you put to the witness now, and again this is part of the summary Mr. McCloskey read into the record. A Serb soldier at the gate telling the men to throw down their things, the identity cards. That is the essence of this sentence. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I said at the beginning that my stenogram might be different from the transcript because I was writing down the translation, the stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No reason --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if you don't want me to ask the question, I needn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have just explained that and I just -- sorry. I'm talking. I just wanted to assist you and put that on the record and I know this is very difficult for you. I understand that. I'm not prohibiting putting questions to the witness, it's your right, but I wanted to assist with you the right wording. There's no need to explain it further. Please put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but I need assistance while the transcript is running so that my notes are not different to the transcript, because I put my questions on the basis of my own notes, and Mr. McCloskey said in translation: "He saw that people were throwing down on the ground all the things that they were carrying with them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to avoid any misunderstanding and any conflict, I was assisting you. Please understand that. I read to you what was to be found in this transcript, and now you know what is in the transcript and now put a question and don't argue with me. That is guidance, and that was assistance for you. Please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was just pointing out the difference between the translation and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, let me ask you this: Did you see the things being thrown onto the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And why did you throw documents away? Why did you discard documents? What was the reason for that? What would have happened to you if you had them on you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first part of the question was already answered twice, but the last question you should answer. What would have happened to you if you had them on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were searched earlier by Serb soldiers if we were carrying anything, other things than -- than we -- than they could see. So that could be a threat that we have different documents with us, different -- I mean, documents from Muslim people carrying along with UN personnel. So that could raise questions, and that could deliver an unsecure situation for us at the moment. At that very moment we were -- we had not any weapons or whatsoever on us, so that was the reason that I made that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, tell us, how could you have carried out your assignment of documenting the fact that nine people had been killed if you didn't have documents telling you who they were and what they were? How could you report back to the forces and your commander that a crime was being committed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The reason for that is it's quite easy. I made some photographs, and that was enough evidence for me to get back to my unit again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, could they have confiscated your camera and all that evidence? Could the Serb soldiers have done that? Yes or no? Could they have confiscated all those things?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible, but it was to me the most valuable thing to hide and that was possible, so -- and carrying a lot of documents with us was not that easy, because wearing only a trouser and a T-shirt and a cap, there is nothing much to hide beneath your clothes any more. So that was the reason that I kept the most valuable thing, and that was my camera at the moment, with me and not the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel, your statement, is it valid if you have no evidence from the scene itself, the so-called scene of crime, as you call it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I think there was a lot of evidence, because I was with two colleagues, a sergeant major of the Royal Netherlands Army and another lieutenant from the Royal Netherlands Army. So we were working there as UN personnel, so we saw with our own eyes what we had seen at that scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, can you tell us this: The UN soldiers from the base, did they carry out dead Muslims around the base, and could they then have portrayed the situation as having been caused by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was simply not possible, because we had very less personnel outside. The personnel that was outside was small groups led by a lieutenant, small groups of ten personnel led by a lieutenant under close surveillance. We had no manpower whatsoever to bring out dead Muslim people because we didn't find any dead Muslim people in the compound or next to the compound by UN personnel other than we reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now may we have 1D53 [as interpreted] displayed, please. Thank you. And while we're waiting for that to appear on e-court, tell us, please, whether you and your group, the group you went with to this location that you photographed, did you find any dead bodies, and did you report back to your command except for the ones that you've mentioned? Thank you. I said 1D953, 1D953. Thank you. Now, my question was whether you and the officers who were with you with those nine dead bodies, did you find any other bodies apart from those dead bodies, and if you so, did you report back to your command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The occasion that I just spoke about and was earlier reported in the summary, that was the only nine bed Muslim people that we saw on the trip to the small stream in -- next to the meadow. We found at that specific timings no other dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now would you take a look at the document in front of you. It is dated the 21st of June, 2011, and it is the -- it says "Defence minister to reveal secret grave." And I quote: "Defence Minister Hans Hillen agreed to reveal the whereabouts of a mass grave in Srebrenica during an interview with TV programme Nieuwsuur on Monday evening. "He was reacting to claims by a former DutchBat soldier that during the Bosnian war in the 1990s seven Muslims died in the Dutch enclave and were buried there. The soldier, Dave Maat told the programme that the Defence Ministry has photos and a map with the co-ordinates of the grave but had refused to release them." And my question to you is this, Colonel: Do you know anything at all about this grave, where is this located, what the co-ordinates are, and how it came into being? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I saw that same news footage on TV as well. During the last two days two people died on the compound, and that were the people that we let enter the enclave -- the -- through the fence that I opened. Two people died over there as I know of. They were buried on the compound itself. Now, this news item here refers to that situation that on the 12th or 13th of July, a few Muslims died and they had to -- they had to be buried, and that happened on the compound itself. I don't know where the Defence Ministry -- why they are not disclosing this -- this fact, because it was well-known also to that soldier that there were no more people buried there. And a lot of soldiers that have problems after -- years later after this happenings, and I know this soldier myself because he was a member of a company of the 3rd platoon and his name is David Maat, I even know his first name, and I know also that he has some problems of coping with the situation of the enclave and the situation that he had afterwards. So he has some mental problems as well. So that is the reason probably that this get in news now and then and is -- yeah, that's the only thing I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Colonel, but you still haven't answered my question in actual fact. Do you know where the grave site is, the one that the Ministry of Defence refers to in the document I just read out and what the coordinates are, and do they coincide perhaps with the co-ordinates where you took photographs of those nine dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, the people were buried on the compound itself, and it were to my knowledge two people. The site that I referred to of the nine bodies is near the Budak hill, near to a stream, and I did some drawings myself here and on the maps where that exactly was. So this is much different than the situation you are describing, and if I may say so, sir, I don't know the co-ordinates by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, can you tell me whether it was by chance that all the evidence was lost about the location where the dead bodies were found, nine dead bodies, and that 16 or 17 years later what the minister said has still not been disclosed about the grave that the command of the Dutch Battalion dug while it was in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't get quite your question, because you're referring now on two different situations. One I explained you already of the nine bodies and where that was. That was exactly not on the compound. And the two Muslim people that I am referring to and also in the Dutch news footage that we see over here is on the compound itself. And I don't know why the minister isn't revealing this news if it is well known. You better ask the Ministry of Defence, because I'm only working as an officer for the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, may I ask you for one clarification. We see on the screen this document of the 21st of June, 2011. In the second paragraph it refers to seven Muslims died in the Dutch enclave and were buried there. There is a difference between the two you are mentioning and these seven, and it is said here "in the Dutch enclave," and not "in the Dutch compound."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you any idea why this could happen, why this is formulated in this way in this Dutch news document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we see after all these years is that people are not tracking the right words, and in the collective memory is -- enclave has been mentioned here in this news footage, but it's also -- but it's merely -- it has to be base or compound, because the two were buried, at least to my knowledge, to -- on the compound. The soldier that is describing of seven is to his knowledge that there could be seven on the compound itself, but I have a colleague who was then a captain, and we spoke about this, and he said that, "We never buried seven people on the compound, only two." And I spoke this colleague only I think two or three weeks ago as I met him, because he was then the company commander of the medical unit that came along with us to the enclave. So that is the only knowledge that I have mixing up words after all these years and reporters telling something in a news footage that I see over here on screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. To avoid any misunderstanding, what I'm asking you is this: Do you know what happened to those seven who were buried in the enclave that the Defence Ministry is referring to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness sit closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not to my knowledge that there were seven men buried in the enclave or on the compound as I just spoke about. The mixing up in words between "enclave" and "compound," I think that here is the question. And that's the only thing that I can say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, could the minister have misinformed the public with imprecise data or is it some other -- other matter, some other case that you don't know about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I simply can't -- can't answer this question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now take a look at what the soldier that you mentioned says, Maat, where he says "16 years." The title is "16 years," that portion. "When Maat revisited the area recently, he discovered that the families of the dead had been looking for the bodies of their loved ones for the past 16 years. On his return, he approached the Defence Ministry and asked for information about the location of the grave but was told this information was confidential. According to Hillen, the ministry misunderstood the question. The DutchBat soldiers were debriefed on their return from Srebrenica, and what they said is confidential. The minister thought Maat wanted this information." Now, my question to you is this: Apart from these seven, were there any more, any others that were buried and which was confidential and whom they informed about upon their return from Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not that I know of. DutchBat or better the UN Battalion, DutchBat III, to my knowledge has not buried any other Muslim people near on the compound or in the enclave itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Other than the two you spoke of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other than two. Sorry, sir. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, could be more precise -- or, rather, since I'm speaking in court, would it be more precise to say that you know of no others apart from those two, but since the minister spoke about it and the soldier spoke about it, then we should ask them and seek information from them? This is fresh information dated the 21st of June, 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is exactly what the witness said. "Not that I know of." He is giving you his knowledge. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't understand. That's why I asked again. So the colonel needn't answer that question. Now could we have 07140 displayed on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that this is a 65 ter number, Mr. Tolimir. Do you tender the last document, the press report, 1D953?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We are tendering document 1D953. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1D953 shall be assigned Exhibit D320. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Colonel, you can probably recognise the general Potocari area and the base. Could you mark where the location was where you photographed those nine dead bodies. Could you mark it in on the map. It was probably close to the base. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, with the assistance of the court usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here. It was here between the bushes, because the bushes are hiding that road that follows through the woods here, and here is a small stream as well, and this is the Budak hill area. So it was quite next to this road here what he -- I'm just marking it out again. This is along the houses, the road, and it is in this wooded area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we take it where you marked at the left part -- wait a moment, please. At the left part of your marking where you made a circle, is that the place where you saw the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's exactly down here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you don't have the floor. Please wait until you get the floor. I'm just talking to the witness. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please put a number 1 near to this circle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Wait please. Wait please. You will get the floor. You know the procedure, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in addition to that, could you please mark, if you recall, where the two Muslims who died in the compound were buried.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the back of the compound as I know of, and it was at the rear side of the compound, and that was more or less at the -- in this area. And I mark a 2 over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Now, Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Colonel, please, would you put a number 2 at the actual location of the base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not preferable, because we have already a number 2. Would you like that the witness uses a number 3 for that? The location of the base as Mr. Tolimir calls it. A number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a total blue marked area that was the compound of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicated that with a number 3. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this into evidence now please and my next question is as follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait. Please wait. You are tendering a document. This marked photograph will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7140, which is Exhibit P2632 marked in court by the witness shall be assigned Exhibit D321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were asked by Judge Nyambe, and we heard from the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief, that you didn't work with refugees at the point where the men were separated from the women. I'd like us to look at document D174 next, please, D174. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the technicians for the e-court material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We now have this document of the United Nations before us, received by Mr. Annan at the United Nations, and it was sent by Mr. Akashi from the UN peace forces in Zagreb. The date is the 11th of July, 1995, and this document concerns UN policy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the second page of this document displayed, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Witness -- accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph (d) [as interpreted], and below that it says and I quote: "After consultations with the Bosnian government and in order to avoid a humanitarian catastrophe, the Bosnian Serbs will be asked to allow all the inhabitants of Srebrenica, including the men, to go to Tuzla if they so wish. The Dutch will be instructed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. In paragraph (d) I can't find this part you are quoting or reading. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 7 of paragraph (b). Paragraph (b), line 7, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me repeat -- or, rather, continue. "The Dutch will be instructed to remain in the Srebrenica enclave at least until arrangements have been negotiated and finalised with Bosnian Serb authorities for the departure from the enclave of those people. Ideally, UNPROFOR will remain an armed and substantial presence in the enclave at least until the departure from the enclave of all those wishing to leave has been completed. This preference will need to be balanced against the Dutch government's desire to evacuate its forces from Srebrenica with the shortest delay. UNPROFOR will with the support of the UNHCR will also endeavour to reach agreement with the Bosnian Serbs to escort any convoy of refugees from Srebrenica to Tuzla." Now, my question to you is this: Was it UN policy to see that the UNPROFOR command in Srebrenica should assist the evacuation of the refugees from Srebrenica going to the territory where they wished to go? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document, and it's quite clear to me that UNPROFOR supports the evacuation of the Muslim people, and that's the only thing I can say about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if this was indeed UN policy, your position was it -- was it then contrary to UN policy at the time when you expressed it and when you told Lieutenant Duijn what you told him?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is a letter from the highest level of the UN. The situation on the ground was much different as you're well aware of. Your personnel were collecting and disarming UN personnel from their weapons, even myself. I was disarmed by your personnel. So there was quite a different situation than the statements here in the letter from the highest level from UN. So on the ground, it was different from what is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you were disarmed because previously you had opened fire on the Army of -- the Republika Srpska Army, not only you but the whole UNPROFOR unit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We did as -- the moment I was disarmed, I was not opening fire. I was merely disarmed because I was a threat to them because I was spreading news over what they were doing next to the road and in the direct environment to the Muslim people. So if you respect this document on one hand and being one of the leaders of the Bosnian -- no, of the VRS army itself, then we have here a typical situation, because your men, as I encountered them, were differently instructed as what -- what I read here in the letter, and they told me myself. So VRS military personnel acted differently from this UN document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'm asking you on the 8th, 9th, and 10th, did you fire at the Army of Republika Srpska in keeping with the orders you had received, in keeping with the green order?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This question -- I myself was not firing, and I cannot comment this question any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we started a bit later today that therefore we have our first break later, but I think now it's time for our first break. We will resume 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I just want to raise one matter. In the meantime, we received a CD with document Exhibit P1301, which was previously marked for identification pending the delivery of the CD. Now it is in front of us. The document is in evidence now, P1301. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Colonel, you said here that you were disarmed, and I asked you if before that you had been at war with the Army of Republika Srpska. You said you knew nothing about it, and you were not involved in any such war. My question is: What about other soldiers who were subordinate to you? Did they really shoot at the VRS soldiers in keeping with order green from the UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: First in what you say, in the first piece of your question, I never said that I did nothing -- that I knew nothing about it, and I also didn't say that I was not involved in any such war, because I was on the ground and there was actually -- actually one of the witnesses on the ground. So I don't know where that came from. But to your question, soldiers who were subordinate to me did not fire at the VRS army. There were some soldiers in my company that fired at the VRS during the 10th and the 9th in the happenings around the blocking positions in the road south to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what Major Franken says. He knew what soldiers did, and he issued the green order. He appeared as a witness in this trial, and in July 2010, and the 1st of July, 2010, on page 3473 the question is: "When did you issue order green?" His answer was: "It must have been on the night of the 9th July." And on page 3475, lines 8 through 10, he says: "As I said before, we were in a state of war with the VRS. We opened fire together with the Muslim army." And to the question: "Was your mandate to destroy VRS weapons and go to war with the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska, after the issuing of the green order?" On page 3484, lines 1 through 3, he says: "No, it was not within our mandate, but again my mandate changed significantly from the moment when the UN ordered me to defend Srebrenica, and that was the reason why I issued the green order. So in that sense, yes." My question to you is: You members of the UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, did you have a mandate to take sides, to side with one of the warring parties and wage war together with that side?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To the specific question from your side, I have to stick also what the Major Franken said. The situation changed dramatically after the 9th of July, so we were forced to protect the Muslim people, to fire at the VRS. So I think that Major Franken made also quite clear that there was a different situation than our initial mandate, and still we was not acting accordingly to the mandate to fire at one of the parties, but nevertheless, to protect the other party we had to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. You are a military man. If somebody's shooting at you, even if it is UNPROFOR, is it logical that at least the minimum step of disarming them should be taken to disable that person or persons from firing at you again?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: You could say that, Mr. Tolimir, but there is one big difference to that, and that is if you disarm the other party, meaning in this situation UNPROFOR, you have to disarm them all, and that was a thing that you did not do with the VRS. You armed [sic] only specific military personnel, meaning UNPROFOR, the ones who got in the way. For instance, me myself, I got in the way of seeing something, of collecting information, and that was the reason why I was disarmed. So more colleagues were disarmed because they saw something or got in the way of the VRS actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that in the examination-in-chief you said you spent one night in isolation, you were put in isolation which by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, he was not examined during examination-in-chief. There was no examination-in-chief. That was the summary read into the record by Mr. McCloskey, just for the record. Now the answer of the witness, please, about the isolation you were put by the Army of Republika Srpska in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was for a short period in isolation, the moment I got disarmed with my men, and shortly afterwards I was brought back to the compound, as earlier stated by Mr. McCloskey in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for saying this, but it was said on page 7 that Captain Mane took you back to the remise, but never mind. Let's not go back to that. My next question would be: Since you said here on page 4 that you had seen people taking food from dumpsters -- sorry. The Prosecutor said that reading the summary. My question is: Is it the case that to this day in all countries in the Balkans, all dumpsters containing waste and rubbish are being gone through to find useful scraps, and it's not as organised as it is in Western countries?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, sir, it was well organised in Srebrenica before it became an enclave, because we even used the formerly dumpster trucks from the municipality of Srebrenica and used them to got rid our own garbage. So they got into the garbage of UNPROFOR because no convoys of the UNHCR came into the enclave anymore because they were stopped by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer this question: Is it the case that to this day in all the countries of the former Yugoslavia people look through dumpsters and waste, generally, to separate various items unless that is organised by the state?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I've been recently not to -- to former Yugoslavia, and also before I was in the enclave I made some several vacation trips to Yugoslavia when it was one state, and it was always well organised. So there were always people searching in dumpsters, but not for food, I reckon. And your country was well organised before the war, the Yugoslavian war, started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for this answer. My question is: Does rummaging through rubbish indicate that somebody's hungry or that they are looking for useful scraps that can be sold or used for another purpose?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Our estimation and our belief and what we saw daily happen when we dumped the trucks also on my personal patrolling along that side to OP Romeo and Quebec where we dumped our garbage that the people were looking for food and not for other items they could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We won't deal with this any more, because all things are possible in war. Can we now look at 65 ter 07144. That is your statement dated 23 July 1995, which is recorded as confidential. I don't know if it's still confidential. Perhaps the Prosecution can tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is Exhibit P2636 now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it that it is not under seal. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we see it on the screen and it's not under seal, I will note again that it is an interview done with you on 23 July 1995, just 13 days after the events in Srebrenica. Here is what you say, I quote from the first line in the first paragraph towards line 13: "I am the patrol co-ordinator for Srebrenica. On the morning of 11 July 1995, there was a rumour in the local refugee camp that seven people had been shot and the bodies were near the well in Potocari. As I was the patrol coordinator, I knew the area very well. I drove with Lieutenant Koster and Sergeant Major Van Schaik to the well. As we approached the well I saw one man running from that direction, and a Muslim woman whom we had asked about the bodies. She pointed us to the direction of the bodies. On arriving at the scene, we saw nine dead men who appeared to have been shot, lying face down with their heads almost in the well. Beside the bodies were passports and ID cards. I gave instructions to Sergeant Major Van Schaik to pick these up, which he did. We then took photographs of the scene, including the bodies. As we were leaving the scene, we heard gunshots, and we saw a Bosnian Serb Army soldier who appeared distracted. I told the sergeant to get rid of the passports and the IDs which he did. The film has been sent to Holland to be developed." My question is: Does this description reflect the actual scene and the event as you experienced it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You go on to say: "On Monday night, people started moving down from the mountains and other areas within the enclave into the DutchBat Compound. The DutchBat housed approximately 25.000 refugees in two compounds. On Tuesday, General Mladic came to the refugee camps with a camera crew." Does this description correspond to what you described?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: If you had driven, as you say in line 4, with Lieutenant Koster and Sergeant Major van Schaik, where was your vehicle when you were passing by the barricades, as you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This report was translated from Dutch into English. We never drove, because we haven't -- we hadn't even got enough fuel for driving because we were patrolling the last few months with donkeys to get to the OPs. So it must be a mistake in the translation of this document, because we had no cars at that moment, and we were not driving with cars from the compound to the site that I spoke about in this document. It was quite near.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If in line 4 we see a mistranslation, is it the case also in line 10 which says: "I gave instructions to the sergeant major to pick these up, which he did." My question is: How did he them up, and what did he put them into? He couldn't just hold them in his hands.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. That's quite true. He picked them up and put these documents -- he looked at them and put them in his camouflage uniform trousers, because we have on even sides pockets on the camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that the way this is written this sounds as if you put these documents into some sort of vehicle? Right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I don't see that like -- no. No. It may be something about translation, but I don't see that. There was simply no vehicle, so we couldn't put it in a vehicle. It is just a mistranslation about walking or driving, and that is no thing that happened in this document, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it then possible that in this part of the statement when it says: "I driver with Lieutenant Koster and sergeant Major van Schaik and I told him to pick them up," is it unclear from this how you travelled there and how he picked these things up? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is again repetition. The witness explained in detail how that could have happened that the word "I drove" came into this statement. Please avoid repetitions. It's a waste of time. Move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Colonel, let us look at line 1 as the President says. It says: "I am the patrol co-ordinator for Srebrenica. On the morning of 11 July 1995, there was a rumour in the local refugee camp that seven people had been shot ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have read -- you have read all of this into the transcript already. There's no need to do that again. Put a question to the within, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I read this out in order to ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the course of this discussion, it was said that you found this out from one of the interpreters. So which version is true? Was it a rumour that circulated around the refugee camp or was it something you found out from one of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: In answer to your question, there were a lot of rumours. That morning there was a lot going on. But specifically answering your question, it came from an interpreter that we got the news of probably the seven men that were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you were told that by an interpreter on the 11th of July, 1995, do you know whether VRS soldiers were at that time at the location where you found the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: As I described earlier and the moment that we came to the site where we find the nine men, at that point where we had to leave, we saw VRS soldier chasing a woman who was running away from a house. And that is in the my other statements as well. So there were VRS personnel in the immediate area that I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not say that soldiers were chasing her. You said that close to that woman you saw a Serb who looked distracted. You did not mention in your statement that the woman was chased by VRS soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was correct what you're saying, but meaning Serb, there were no other Serbians not in uniforms around at that moment. There were only VRS personnel around near the road and near the houses that I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If this happened on the 11th, as you say in your statement, is it possible that these men had been killed on the 10th during combat before the VRS came to the area of Potocari and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Sir, if I may say so, I answered this question earlier, because the moment we came to the nine bodies, they were warm and the blood was still running, and a day later a body is not warm any more, and the blood isn't running, because temperature at that moment was almost 30 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Colonel, but that was on the 11th. If the temperature was so high, was the VRS close to your base in Potocari, because in the same statement, you say: "On Monday night, people started moving down from the mountains and other areas within the enclave," and then three lines below you say: "On Tuesday, General Mladic came." If General Mladic came on Tuesday, could the troops have been there on the 11th, on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There was already VRS personnel in the enclave pouring down from the hills as I described earlier. This question was asked earlier for the same dates. So I'd -- they were around. Your personnel was around on the 11th already before the Mladic came to the bus remise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, when did the air-strikes against Bosnian Serb positions in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica occur, on what day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was also on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us were you able to inform the VRS about it on the same day as well as your commander, and does that feature in your reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, because you know as a soldier that I, as a UN member, the VRS is not in my chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that, but were you able to report on that on the 11th and to keep in touch with the VRS while combat was going on and while -- while the air-strikes were still underway, while you were firing at the VRS?
