utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The reports that I made were directly to my commander and even to the battalion commander, so everything was reported, but not to the VRS, because as I stated earlier, the VRS was not in my chain of command. I don't see the -- I don't get your question quite well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, should the VRS be blamed for something that happened before the 11th, before the VRS came to Potocari, or should this be blamed on someone else who was there on the site?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were a lot of happenings before the 11th, and the air-strikes came in in the early morning, and that was on their -- is the VRS accountable? Because the shelling of the compound and the -- they came in from the south in the enclave, the VRS, was the days before the 11th. So the VRS was actually entering the -- entering the enclave before the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On what positions and at what time was the VRS bombed in the enclave during the 11th? Where were those positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't understand your answer -- or your question, because you're saying, "At what time was the VRS bombed?" I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct. At what time did the air-strikes occur against the VRS positions in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't have the exact timings right now by heart, I don't know, but it was in the early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sorry, could you say for the record which day -- date it was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge right now, it's on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the VRS was bombed on the 11th on access points to the enclave, is it possible that on the 11th in the morning or just before when you saw these bodies they were already in Potocari? Could these bodies have been victims or casualties of combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: As I described earlier in my statements, this was -- they were shot quite nearby with small-calibre weapons, and as the way they were laying in the meadow with their faces down to the -- to a small stream, it was quite clear to us, not only to me but also to my colleagues, that they were executed on that place, and it was nothing what looked like that there was a fight going on or was going on at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that somebody killed someone on the 11th in the morning before you arrived, or during the night perhaps, between the 10th and the 11th, because they didn't want to defend their positions or because they weren't withdrawing from their positions or for some other reason? Might they have been killed at that way?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I described earlier that these bodies were -- it was -- they were -- I described it that the bodies were still warm and the blood running, so it couldn't happen the night earlier. So I don't know where you're aiming at, but this couldn't happen earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that the Muslims in front of your UNPROFOR soldiers killed soldiers next to your APCs? They killed their own soldiers right in front of your APCs. Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know about the case of the killing of soldier Rensen and whether any incident took place at that time between a BH Army soldier and a soldier belonging to UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber what this was all about, this incident, what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At that time that that happened, it wasn't quite clear to us what had happened exact -- exactly, but one of the soldiers that was above the turret of the APC got injured at the moment the UN APC was withdrawing from a position. Later on we heard that possibly BH Muslim soldiers could have been responsible for that. And that was at the time that we were in the enclave that I heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And the debriefing -- during debriefing, did you hear statements by eyewitnesses, and did they say how the soldier was killed, how soldier Rensen was killed? Did you hear about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I heard about that -- I heard about that, but I never heard -- personally spoke to the colleagues that were involved in that -- were in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you actually did hear, because you didn't talk to any eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I heard that BH soldiers possibly could have killed soldier van Rensen at the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the soldiers of BH killed UNPROFOR soldiers for withdrawing from their positions, is there the possibility that they might have killed their own soldiers, members of the BH Army, their own combatants, to prevent them from withdrawing faced with the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: You say UNPROFOR soldiers. It was just one soldier, but one too many, I think. So I have to correct that. And then I'm not aware of, as I earlier stated, that BH soldiers shot down their own man. So that is enough questions. I don't think that it's the right point now, 16 years later, to do an estimation of what BH soldiers could have done then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Since you say that, why do you think that they must have been killed by the Serbs if you have not a shred of evidence as to who shot at them and if there are no eye-witnesses? How is that possible, then? How can you arrive at that conclusion then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you now referring again to the nine dead bodies the witness testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's right, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If it was your conclusion that the nine bodies were killed by the Serbs, did you have any evidence that they were actually killed by the Serbs, or did you have any eye-witnesses which would lead to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I explained earlier that we saw Serb soldiers running around quite near to that area. There were no other Muslim armed personnel that we saw in the direct vicinity of that area, and clearly Serb forces were in control of that area. There was no other military personnel in the direct vicinity. So -- and what I earlier stated, they were shot a few minutes ago, the moment we came. So -- or shortly. So it is -- yeah. It is to me quite unbelievable, because we never encountered any Muslim military personnel around that area on the 11th any more. So I never said that I'm sure that VRS personnel could have done that, but all the things that I said earlier lead -- leads to this conclusion, and that was the question you asked me earlier, if I could -- on what basis I made this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you protect the woman that the Serb was chasing, as you said, who had been distracted, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had no -- at that time she was running away, we had no possible means to protect her, because we were unarmed ourselves at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 11th in the morning, were you disarmed or did you have weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We were already disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber at what time you were disarmed on the 11th in the morning and who disarmed you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I said earlier that a group of the Captain Mane disarmed me. I don't have the exact timings any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Captain Mane, did he come to Potocari, to your base on the 11th in the morning to disarm you, or was the situation different?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: He was already on the 11th near the road to the place where the blocking positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the 11th in the morning, was there a blockade along the road? Was there a blockade put up on the road? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There was a blockade southward to -- in the direction of Srebrenica, and that was formed by APCs, and it was controlled by the Lieutenant van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are we talking about the place that you marked right next to the base? Is that what you're talking about, or are you talking about another location controlled by the colonel and some other -- the captain and some other barricade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was somewhat southwards, because it was just in front of the bus remise, if you know the exact point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. But according to what you've said so far, all the witnesses and everything else, nobody says that Colonel Mane was there and the Army of Republika Srpska was by the base. Everybody says that that was on the 12th, after the agreement had been signed on the evacuation, the agreement between the Muslim civilian population, General Mladic, and Colonel Karremans. Do you remember that perhaps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And do you remember when Colonel Karremans had a meeting with the Muslims to inform them that there would be bombing of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was earlier than the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that have been the 10th, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It could have been, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If it was indeed on the evening of the 10th and the incident with the nine dead bodies on the morning of the 11th, do you remember whether it could have been the Army of the Republika Srpska who was next to your -- which was next to your base and had control points at the time of the bombing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Sorry, what is your question, sir? I don't see the question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question is: The Army of Republika Srpska, could it have held the control point, the check-point, with its APC in Potocari right next to your base on the 11th in the morning, when you on the 11th were by the nine dead bodies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: You're bringing everything out of context, because I walked through that blockade to get to the position of where the nine -- where I found the nine people somewhat higher uphill to the Budak area. So I don't see your point right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for having to repeat. On the 11th of July, 1995, in the morning, rumours went around the camp saying that seven people were killed and that their bodies were next to the stream by Potocari. Since I was the co-ordinator of the patrol, I knew the area well, and I drove off with Colonel Konings [phoen]. Now, is it possible that you could have gone there since there was no Army of Republika Srpska and that that might have been in the morning before the bombing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I'd like to remind you, could the soldiers of Republika Srpska have been in your base with NATO deciding to bomb the Serbs later? Would that have been an absurdity or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't see the question. I don't understand the question here. He's asking me something that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me put it this way -- or, rather, let's look at D20. It's the debriefing on Srebrenica. Page 38, please, paragraph 3.58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, at this point in time may I ask you, had been the VRS in the UN compound, in the base itself, at that point in time when the NATO bombing started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not in the compound itself on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could -- I mean, the testimony and the summary of the testimony and the dates thereof have been completely left out, and we're concentrating on a early statement where July 11th was mentioned. If the questions can be put in the context of what's happening on the ground, I think this will be -- make more sense for the Trial Chamber and everyone else, because the dates by themselves can be confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, try to make clear to which specific time you are referring and continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Mr. McCloskey, for your assistance. I'd like to ask the witness to take a look now at paragraph 3.58 that we have on our screens, and since I can't read English very well, perhaps he could read the text from the third sentence on, and then I'm going to tell him how I understand this passage. Perhaps I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should explain for the witness on which kind of document he is looking now so that he can understand the context. You're just saying "debriefing," but you should explain to him what kind of document it is. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he could also briefly see the 11th and the 12th so we can put this in the context of -- of -- of what this is about as opposed to just a few lines that says the 10th, because I -- it's easy to say particular dates, but without the context it doesn't mean much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the witness looking at, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness is looking at is debriefing on Srebrenica provided by the members of his battalion when they arrived in Assen, and it was conducted in Assen in 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, we're reading what actually happened on that 11th of July. It says: "At around noon on Tuesday, the 11th of July," the fourth line down. I'm reading from the fourth line. "At around noon on Tuesday, the 11th of July." May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I quote: "At around noon on Tuesday, the 11th of July, a number of shells struck the area near the armoured vehicle. The abandoned OP (Observation Post) was also shelled. Chaos prevailed among the BH. Internal fighting broke out once again. That evening, the OP crew were permitted to leave because they were willing to take the wife and children of a local BH leader with them," and so on. My question is the following: Can we see from this that on the 11th fighting was still going on right up until the evening, as it says here? Is that evident from this passage? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is OP Mike where you're referring to. I know personally the sergeant who was commanding that APC and this OP. We had given him the order by our operations room to leave OP Mike because a lot of VRS shelling was going on, and it is exactly what's described here, because it was VRS shelling that he had to fall back again from the OP Mike, and he took along family members of the BH leader. There was chaos going on at that moment, and it was quite clear to us in the operations room as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Further down it says: "When the two BiH soldiers with the anti-tank weapons attempted to prevent their departure, they were shot in the head by the BH leader." So the BH leaders shot their own soldiers; is that right? That's my question. Did the BH leaders shoot their own soldiers in the head?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is a statement, I think, from Sergeant Mueller who was then the OP commander at the spot. I know him very well, and he made that decision to leave OP Mike, and -- and there were people shot amongst BH personnel, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that happen on the 11th of July? And everything described here in this paragraph, did it all happen on the evening of the 11th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a problem with the 92 ter. The testimony of this witness as it came into court is that these bodies happened on the 13th of July, and that's what the summary says. Now, there has been one statement which General Tolimir has fairly brought up where this witness has said on the 11th of July, but there's clearly just a mix-up in numbers, and -- and I think that needs to be addressed now. I've -- I've not objected up until this time, but now it's getting beyond -- beyond any -- any sense. He needs to address the issue, I believe, of his testimony in this court along the lines that he's always testified into what happened the 11th, 12th, and 13th, and that's when the bodies happened. So that's what's on -- that's what it's in his evidence. If he's going to question him on that, he needs to put that to him. Fair enough that he can put the statement from the debriefing where he says 11th to him as well, but it's only fair to the witness to put both to him and let the witness sort it out as opposed to assuming that the 11th is the date each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber understand your position. However, it's the right of the accused to put different documents to the witness and to conduct his cross-examination the way he wishes, and especially this witness seems to be very capable to distinguish between different events happened -- which happened in July 1995 in this area. You may deal with that again in your re-examination. Sir, but I would like to refer you again to the question of

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did that happen on the 11th of July? And you may explain what is your recollection on that, if you recall the context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I -- could Mr. Tolimir put up this question again, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's no problem. Your last answer was: "This is a statement," you think, "from Sergeant Mueller," I think you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mueller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "Mueller, who was then OP commander at the spot. I know him very well, and he made that decision to leave OP Mike. And there were people shot amongst BH personnel, yeah." That was your response. And Mr. Tolimir asked you: "Did that happen on the 11th of July?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: If this was on the 11th of July, this situation at the OP, could the base have been blocked on the 11th of July, of your command and your unit in Potocari, blocked by Captain Mane and the other Serb soldiers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to -- to say something about the sequence of the blockings, because on the night earlier, I was also outside at the bus remise. So it's difficult for me to say something about the exact timings after 16 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please, since you said a moment ago that on the 11th you threw away these documents, can documents be thrown away -- or if the Serbian soldiers did not confiscate them from you, and did you throw away documents that were evidence of some event that had taken place or were hiding something, or were they thrown away for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question and make it shorter. On the 11th, the morning of the 11th, in -- when you returned from the location where you had photographed the dead, did you have to give up their -- throw away their passports and ID cards if there was no check-point between there and Potocari to confiscate the IDs and passports? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I said earlier about the timings and dates. It's quite difficult for me to -- after 16 years to get that exactly in timings, as you are asked specifically right now referring to other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer and for all the answers given in this statement 07144, but you gave that statement on the 23rd July 1995, just after the events when your memory was fresh. That's why I just wanted to confirm yes or no. Was this statement given on 23rd July 1995? Could we please display 65 ter 07144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is now P2636. P636.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lieutenant. Did you give this statement on 23rd July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I with like to tender this statement. Oh, I see. It is already an exhibit with a P number. Thank you. I apologise. I thank Mr. Rensen, and I don't want to discuss this statement any more. Mr. Rutten. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now I should like to move to a different set of questions. You have been asked here whether you had a difference of opinion with your mates about the involvement of UNPROFOR in the evacuation. I should like to take a look together with you at what Mr. van Duijn says and then to hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we display 65 ter 07162.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at page 9 in e-court. It's page 13 in English. Page 9 in Serbian. The first line. Paragraph 2 in English. "The witness made contact with Captain Groen who said that he should arrange it." Now, let us look at the last line on page 8. It says: "The first option was that the Serbs organise the deportation, and the second option that the UN organise it. The witness made contact with Captain Groen who said that he should arrange it." My question to you is: Did Captain Groen order van Duijn to organise this evacuation from Srebrenica as we see in this statement on the page that is displayed on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that at the time I was in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Mr. Van Duijn tell you when you asked him who ordered it that he had no time to explain it to you? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at page 10, under "14 July." It begins on page 14 in English and continues on page 15. I quote -- third page in Serbian. "The buses came rather quickly. " It's the next page in English. "The Serbs were still not there. They started filling the buses. Men were boarding the buses, too, while there were no Serbs there. This lasted for about two and a half hours. "At this point, some MSF personnel had arrived who had set up a facility for the wounded." My question is: Did UNPROFOR members themselves organise the evacuation from Potocari without any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you left out two small sentences while you were quoting from this document. I will read that. "The Serbs arrived at 8.30 hours. They just went on." Now you may answer the question of Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were already Serbs there. That's the thing I wanted to stress. And my colleague, van Duijn, started to organise in a correct manner that the Muslim refugees could leave the enclave as they were eager to leave the enclave, because they were in a rather nasty situation at the moment. And that was what I witnessed that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, from 6.30 to 8.30, did your colleague Mr. van Duijn organise the boarding of buses and the evacuation alone, without any presence of Serbs, and the men were boarding buses at that time as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At that moment I wasn't present because that was the same morning that I was in the operations room, and later on I -- that morning I went outside to go to the blocking positions where van Duijn was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did your colleague van Duijn participate together with Serbs in putting people on buses, those refugees how were leaving Potocari to the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in keeping with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: He with his UN personnel, and "he" I mean Lieutenant van Duijn, wasn't actually putting Muslim people on buses. He was just looking at it and to guide it in an orderly manner, that no one would get harmed by VRS personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Doesn't he say that for two full hours -- two and a half hours, in fact, he organised the evacuation himself? Is that what he says or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is a statement that he made himself, so he is responsible for his own statements, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us then look at another statement where he says the same thing, and before that I should like to tender this one. 07 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this statement that we see on the screen be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. This is the statement of the witness van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7162 shall be assigned Exhibit D322. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up 65 ter 07159.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's another statement of Mr. van Duijn's given to the International Tribunal for Criminal Prosecution on the 25th of October, 1995. And since you see this cover page, let us go to page 5, paragraph 6. That's page 6 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar. Paragraph 4. In fact, let's first see who is the man he was talking to. He's talking about a certain Mane. "By talkie-walkie, I informed Captain Groen. Soon after, a man in camouflage approached me. His assistants introduced him as Mane, commander of the military police battalion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Platoon, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "He was about 1.85 metres tall with a corpulent build and short brown hair. He was 29 years of age. We conferred about the deportation of the refugees. At that stage a number of trucks and buses were already parked in readiness on the road outside the compound. I arranged with him that we would concern ourselves with the refugees. He would tell us how many people could be allowed through to the buses. When the moment came, we co-operated in this way, and as the contact between us had gone quite well, I was able to ensure that families were kept together as much as possible." My question is: Are you aware that there was an understanding between van Duijn and Captain Mane, military police commander, that the evacuation would be organised by UNPROFOR; whereas, Mane would only determine the number of people allowed to board the buses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was aware of that, but the problem here is my colleague van Duijn, and that was the dilemma we had together and we spoke about, that he got in a situation where he did not see the total context of what was really happening along the road. So working together with the VRS expelling - or evacuate - people from the enclave could have been easily seen as UN helping to work together with the VRS for ethnic cleansing. So that was the discussion I had with my colleague, and as colleagues among each other, I tried to coach him in a way that he would understand, but at that very moment he was not in a situation that he could understand that. And that was what I tried to do down the road, because I had a perfect overview of what was really happening, and he was right in the middle of that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our second break now, and we will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, you here, and the Judges asked their questions, but anyway, you objected to your colleague van Duijn for co-operating with the evacuation. Now, did you know whether that was perhaps an order given by Major Franken and other superior officers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Later I heard that that was an order, but not at that specific moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the record, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let's look at 65 ter 07160 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have still on the screen 65 ter 7159. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7159 shall be assign Exhibit D323. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at 65 ter 07160 next, please. Page 17 in English. It's a report, a conversation with van Duijn conducted by Mr. Bakker on behalf of the parliamentary commission engaged in the investigation of Srebrenica on the 11th of November, 2002, in Holland, in The Hague, the parliament in The Hague. And may we take a look at page 17 in English now, please, and it's page 14 in Serbian. It's the fourth entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I quote Mr. van Duijn: "When five minutes later things calmed down, I contacted the operative centre of the battalion straight away and asked for Major Franken. I then pointed out what I have actually already said, that we would stay there, and he said that he agreed with that because it fitted in with humanitarian aid. He also asked whether I still needed any more equipment and people. It was clear to him that at the time I was still -- it was still not clear to me that the refugees would have to go away. So he therefore said, 'I know about it. Stay there and just say when you need anything.'" Now, since you answered in the affirmative to this question already, all I can ask you is this -- or, rather, put the question a different way. From this does it follow that Major Franken ordered van Duijn to remain during the evacuation of the refugees, to remain at the location where the evacuation was taking place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document and I read it, what you already read in to this courtroom, and I heard it, and that's what I'm just seeing here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now take a look at page 19 of this same statement, 65 ter 07160. Or, rather, it's 19 in the Serbian and 23 in the English. Thank you, Aleksandar. And then we can move on to page 24 of the English when we've looked at page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the entry where van Duijn is talking and -- talking about the problem, how it came about in relations between him and those with photographs. "Of course --" I'm reading the third line from the top. "Of course, but that wasn't the intention of -- of course, but at the time that was not the intention which I got from the man who I sent away then; Lieutenant Rutten did not have a camera round his neck when he came. He didn't, in fact, tackle me then, and --" Next page, please. "I said I was ready to explain everything to him but that I didn't have time. He then got into a discussion with the Serbian fighters who were standing there. The result of this was that I had to explain to the Serbian commander why the Serbian fighters were called Nazis. He also reacted very emotionally to this. He said to me, 'My father fought with Tito's Partisans against the Nazis, so I don't want to be called a Nazi.'" That is what a Serb soldier said. I forgot to emphasise that. Now, my question is this: Did you really call the Serbian soldiers Nazis, and was that why there was a conflict between you and the soldier and that is what van Duijn refers to here?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was actually a discussion that I had with my colleague, and the Serbs were interfering at that very point, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether this was proper for you to call Serb soldiers Nazis or not? So were you biased in your reactions there, or were you guided by something else to refer to them in that way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was guided by something else. I said earlier that I did some discoveries along the road, and van Duijn was not aware of my discoveries. He said that also in the same statement that is here in front of us that he thought that I was quite clean when I came to that point, but the thing was I wasn't clean as he described it. I earlier saw things happen that to me seemed to me quite differently than as he estimated the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let's see what Mr. van Duijn says about that on page 20. It's the same page in English. We're reading the second entry. Asked by Mrs. Heringa, van Duijn says: "After Lieutenant Rutten had tackled me, he started talking to the Serbian soldiers saying, 'This is like what happened 50 years ago with the Nazis.' The Serbs understood this as being branded as Nazis. They thought this was unacceptable. That was why one of them pointed out that his father had fought with the Serbian troops with Tito against the Nazis. I got Colonel Kremer to escort Lieutenant Rutten back to the camp. Then I was confronted by the Serbian commander asking me, 'Why are you branding us as Nazis?' The result of all this was that the transportation had to be stopped for one and a half hours. Because of this, our soldiers had to intervene because people were collapsing at temperatures of about 30 degrees Centigrade. This caused a lot of problems." Did Colonel Kremer take you away from this place where you had a confrontation with the Serbian soldiers over the use of the term "Nazi"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I came along with Colonel Kremer and I spoke with him, and he had the same opinion as I had, but he said he cannot do something else at this very moment. And we spoke about that, about the situation that was along -- happening along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have any other personal confrontations with your colleague van Duijn, or was this clash over your difference of opinion on this one issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had a clash of a difference of opinion, and I tried to explain him what I was seeing through the camera when I was along -- alongside the road, and that was not a good view if you look through the camera in what the -- what the UN personnel was, in fact, could have been seen actively helping to -- to -- with the deportation of the UN -- with the Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But Mr. van Duijn says that he had managed to save many families from being separated, and when he objected, only those who were older than 18 were separated or below age 60, according to his agreement with Captain Mane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's not correct, because I was in the white house, and I made some pictures of very young men who were in the house, even boys that were in the house in -- in the second floor of the white house in the opposite of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you said that it was not so, tell me, how many soldiers in total were taken away from the white house? How many prisoners of war were removed from there, just to determine how many were separated.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Let me first correct something. They were not prisoners of war, because when we in military establish a line to clarify who is a prisoner of war, we have an exact procedure of identify who is combatant and noncombatant. If -- as we know of in earlier statements, you saw in front of the white house every man that came in had to throw down his belongings and also the sets of ID. So that's the reason I object to the word "prisoners of war," because to my opinion we have there in military a different procedure for that. That's the first thing. The moment I got into the house, as you said, they were not youngsters that were in the house. I myself, together with the Sergeant Major van Schaik saw that there were youngsters on the second floor in that house. So the situation that van Duijn describes is his statement, and I am now saying what my opinion was along the road, and history now is saying to me - and we can read it all - that the 8.000 peoples or 7.000 were found dead afterwards, so I don't see the point here right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you, those 7- or 8.000 people, did they pass through the white house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not all, but a few hundred did pass the white house, because you asked me exact figures. I didn't count them. It were a few hundred, because several times buses full of men left the white house, and that is also in my statement. The other men, as you're well aware of, were leaving earlier the enclave on their own on another road near the Jaglici area and near Milici area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a clarification really. At page 70, lines 13 to 16, you said: "They were not prisoners of war, because when we in military establish a line of -- a line to clarify who is a prisoner of war, we have an exact procedure of identifying who is a combatant and noncombatant." So what were they, these people, according to your military procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people to me were all refugees and people who lived -- civilians who lived in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please let us look at 65 ter 07142 to see what you exactly said in your statement because I was unfair asking you about numbers that you said you can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are tendering 65 ter 7160; is that correct? Because that was not a statement but an interview by a parliamentary commission. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7160 shall be assigned Exhibit D324. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to note that the last two documents were not on the list of documents to be used during the cross-examination of this witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the statement was on the list, 65 ter 07142, we could see it in e-court, if not, then we don't need to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 07142 has already been assigned Exhibit P2634. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was referring to the last two documents. They were not on the list. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we now look at P2364 [as interpreted]. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P2634.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now look at page 5 to see what the witness told the Prosecution on page 5. Paragraph 2 in Serbian. That's page 5 in English, page -- sorry, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "It was clear that this could not go on. I went to see Major de Haan, the Dutch UNMO official, but it was to no avail. Together with Sergeant Major Rave, I tried to arrange the release of some of those in the house. The Muslim men held until the house were frightened to death. My impression was that the evacuation of some would not improve the situation, but as it was, the situation was untenable. I then went to one of the Serbian leaders and told him that he aught to arrange something for the evacuation of the Muslim men. The Serb arranged for two buses to be driven to the house. The men from the house filled the buses, and I think there were 60 to 70 in each. I heard later that the men were taken to Bratunac. The house remained full even after this evacuation." My question is: If there were two bus with 60 to 70 men in each, does that mean that the total was between 120 to 140 men taken to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: On this specific occasion, yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you talking about 13th here, 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That could be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If that many people left on the 13th, was it possible that some more left on the 13th if you had your soldier monitoring the buses and escorting the buses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, please, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have a soldier whom you assigned to monitor the buses and to determine how many were leaving on buses towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a driver who was standing on call. That was a Private Verbugt who was -- I asked him to count the number of buses and trucks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my question is this: Since they didn't -- weren't evacuated with the civilians, were they prisoners of war and taken from the white house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: These were to me, as I earlier stated, they were civilians. They were men and youngsters and were earlier separated along the bus line by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with your opinion, but once they'd separated them, did they tell you why they were separating them, why they weren't going with the civilians? Did they give any reason for this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Because they were males between the age of 12, 13 years old and 60, I think, in total, yes. And that was the reason. All men that could have been BH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of the Serb soldiers answer the question of why they were being separated, the men from the women? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: They said that it was for interrogation purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we now go back to 65 ter 07160. It is D324 now. It's the stenographic report of the Hearing of the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry on Srebrenica held on Monday, the 11th of November, 2002, in the old Assembly room of the Lower House of the States General in The Hague. And I'm interested in page 25. Actually, it's page 30 in English and 25 in Serbian. Thank you. Let's look at van Duijn's answer to Mr. Bakker's question. It says: "Yes. It says in the report that I had driven over people were my armoured vehicle. That is not correct. It's not true. It is true that during the return trip, people fell off two armoured vehicles. This was not my armoured vehicle but the other armoured vehicle that, together with mine, took over more and more small blocking positions to protect the convoy of refugees. As soon as the armoured vehicles were stationary, people fell off the front of the vehicle." Now, my question to you is this: Did you -- were you blaming Mr. van Duijn of this as he said earlier on in response to Mr. Bakker's question? Do you blame him for that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is at hindsight what I'm reading now, so that's -- in the week in July that we speak about, I was not aware of the fact that -- that this happened, but I was aware of the fact that APCs from our company were trying to protect the civilians that were coming out from Srebrenica towards Potocari to the bus remise and later on as part of them to the compound, and that was a very chaotic situation, but what exactly is described down here, I wasn't aware of that in the moment -- in the first week of July in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what you mean by the term "remise"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The remise is the bus -- the old bus remise, bus station, you could call it, quite near to the UN compound near Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything at all about whether somebody was run over or whether it was as Mr. van Duijn describes it? Was anybody run over when the refugees were transported from the firing positions to the base?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At that moment in July, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know now at this point in time whether anybody was run over when the refugees were transported? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, but there was another occasion when they fell back from OP Mike with an APC there. People were hit by an APC I heard later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the number? How many, and what was the fate of those people? Were they just hit, or did they die as a result?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm not exactly aware of these happenings any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell me this: Does UNPROFOR and the Dutch Battalion, does it have any records showing how the people were killed, the people they know were killed, and that they were on the spot, on the actual spot?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we have a list of names found in the grave that the ministry referred to? Is there a list? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What kind of grave are you referring to, Mr. Tolimir? I would like to understand your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the grave that was mentioned on the 26th of July this year by the minister. He said that it was confidential, and we admitted the document into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is the reason why I asked. First you refer to the ministry instead of the minister, and the second was I think you heard a lot of answers by this witness. He can't give you a list of more than at the most two buried people there because he doesn't know anything about others. You should rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I won't rephrase it, because I've already received an answer. I have no further questions for this witness. So, Colonel, thank you for coming and answering my questions. I thank you for all that, and I wish you every success in your military career, and I'm happy to see you here in uniform, because you're the first -- actually, the second witness who has come into this courtroom in uniform. So thank you. The Defence rests. We have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President. We thank all the participants in today's proceedings, and that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and I will try to -- to get through this in the time we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, you were very -- on the chronology and the dates, the general showed you, I think it was the first report you made just a few days after your experience in the enclave where you suggest on the 11th of July you see the bodies, and we went over your summary of your previous testimony where you had been consistently [sic] with your chronology of the bodies happening on the 13th of July. Is it possible you've been confused a bit by the actual dates of these events?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The problem is, and I reckon this to my own responsibility, that 16 years later, it's hard to define whether it was on the 11th, 13th, or 12th, but the sequence of happenings was as I described here in front of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as the summary reflected those sequences on the 10th, the 11th, the 12th, the 13th, to the best of your recollection, was that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also said on page 70 that you had a different procedure for POWs, and when you were telling the general that the Serb soldiers were making the men and boys throw their -- their belongings and ID away. Can you just describe us briefly how your forces would appropriately determine whether someone was a combatant or a noncombatant?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we put up a line to identify whether they have personal belongings that could relate to if they are military or not, and that could happen with ID cards, with tags, with everything that relates to if you're working within the military or not. If you have other IDs, meaning that you could be a civilian, for instance, you collect working permits of local personnel, then it's quite clear that they were not in the military. So we set up this line of identifying who is military or not to later on use it in the interrogation that follows that first identifying moment of people that you collect and military that you collect during a -- an action so to get a perfect view of what units are involved and what personnel is involved in the action that has military been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So by requiring the men to dispose of their IDs and then burn them like you've described, would that reflect any serious interest in determining whether or not the men were in the military?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. Then you -- in fact you are saying that you don't have any interest at all in identifying who you are collecting. The only reason that I can imagine to do that is to get rid of not only the personal belongings by burning it and the ID cards by burning it but also of the people itself, because that is the natural way of -- to get rid of every piece of evidence that you have from the people that you're collecting and actually deporting from the enclave. That was my opinion at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If your army took several busloads of young boys and men into custody, would you also be required under -- well, any sense of humanity as well as the Geneva Conventions to provide them with food, water medical help?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, we are obliged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. Colonel Rutten, a moment ago you said it is - 84, page 84 [as interpreted] of the transcript, line 13 - that there were boys aged 12 and 13. How were you able to establish the age of these boys? Did you have access to proof by which you could establish how old they were with certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I refer to what I saw in the white house, and these were sons of the men who were also in the white house, and the moment I make -- made pictures on the second floor in that white house, I could easily see that there were youngsters and by the age that I already referred to. So I was -- my own age was then, in 1995, 35 years old, and I can easily see then who is approximately 12 or 13 or 14 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we all agree that it was a reference to page 74 and not 84, just to have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's right. I said page 74, line 13. And it's where the witness was speaking about boys age 12 and 13. But thank you for your answer, Witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination here in this trial. Thank you very much that you came here to testify and to help us with establishing the truth. Thank you very much again, and now you are free to return to your normal activities. Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
